text: Serik Nurgaliyev (Kazakh) / Age: 30
Rank/Position: Red Army soldier, light machine gunner (DP)
Civilian Occupation: Miner / ore extractor (Karaganda region)
Origin: Kazakh SSR (Central Asian steppe / East)
As the enemy soldier's head disappears in a blood-red burst under Serik's fire, the
Kazakh machine-gunner thinks about the dreams he used to have
back home. Down in the mines, bending in the dark, he used to daydream about seeing the world
one day. This was not what he meant. He hadn't imagined being dragged, against his will, to a foreign
place. A place where life, if possible, was even more miserable than it had been before. But that
is exactly what happened.
And Serik calms himself with a single thought:
even if some miracle sent him back in time,
he still wouldn't be able to change the outcome.
He had been helpless from the moment the draft officers
appeared at the mine and announced they had three hours to pack.
Three hours to put their affairs in order before they left
“to help cleanse Mother Russia of the Western invaders.”
Serik didn't want to look stupid, so he didn't ask who these Western invaders were, or why
Mother Russia needed cleansing from them.
And he decided it was even smarter not to ask what any of it had to do with him — a Kazakh.
So he did what everyone in his shift did.
He went home. As they walked through the snowy
street, Serik saw out of the corner of his eye his neighbor as he broke into a run and
headed for the nearby forest. That was not an option for Serik. Deserters would be
hunted down. Or, if they weren't, they would freeze to death out there. Serik had a family.
So he chose the path that had the best chance of bending back into itself and leading him home again.
He went into the house.
He gathered what he thought was essential.
Then he held Gaukhart — and their seven-month-old baby, Ainur — as if there might be no tomorrow.
Because there very easily might not be for him.
With Ainur's sweet baby scent still in his nose, Serik set out with the men of the village.
The draft officers escorted them on both
sides. After a short walk — seven kilometers — they reached the district
assembly point, where the trains departed. The train ride felt miserable. Serik and
hundreds of others were crammed into a single car like sardines. After the first
few hours, the stench of urine and shit saturated everything — men giving up on cleanliness because there
was no other choice. But the worst was yet to come.
Days later, the train was forced to stop in the middle of nowhere. The rails ahead had
been eaten apart by the cold. What followed was the hardest four and a half weeks of
Serik's life. Which is saying something,
considering that since the age of twelve he had broken stone, lifted impossible weights,
and bent over in hellish heat for fourteen-hour shifts. The heat was the first thing he started to miss.
Wading through knee-deep snow tested him at first. Then it became worse.
Everything on him soaked through. His limbs began to numb, then stiffen.
Each step turned into an impossible task. In the first days, he kept himself alive by picking a
point in the distance and telling himself: “If I reach that, this ends.” A week later, he could
no longer afford even that. He focused only on his steps. One after another. The smallest unit of value
he had left. He told himself that as long as he could keep that rhythm, he would be
fine. One of the men from his village — Nur, the baker — had three toes cut off. Two from
his right foot, one from his left. The frostbitten little pieces looked like wild berries.
The sight made Serik's stomach lurch,
bile rising into his throat.
Nur lived for two more days. With toes missing, he staggered.
He fell constantly.
The officers and the others kept hauling him back up,
again and again.
Then one night, two men took him under the arms
and led him into the darkness beyond the campfire.
And they beat him to death.
Serik heard the muffled screams. The dull, heavy thuds.
The next day, he asked a senior man whether it wouldn't have been kinder to shoot Nur.
The answer was simple:
you can't waste ammunition.
After that, Serik stopped asking questions.
He didn't speak again on the road.
He was afraid that opening his mouth would waste energy. He did nothing but concentrate on one step
following another. By the time they reached the Urals, nearly two-thirds of the column
were gone. Serik was almost certain he was the only one from his village who had survived.
And now he couldn't be sure how long his luck would hold. It looked like they were winning
against the Hungarians dug in on the far bank. But what
happens when those men are ground down?
Where would they be sent next?
How much farther would he have to march?
When would he lose his fingers, too?
Or God forbid, his arms or legs?
After everything, would the people at home even recognize him if he ever made it back?
Gaukhart might. Maybe.
He wasn't even sure of that. But to Ainur, he would be a stranger.
A ghost. A pale imprint of whoever he used to be.
He is pulled out of his thoughts by another scream — another enemy crying out in pain under
Serik's fire.
Serik doesn't like thinking about how many little girls like Ainur he has already made into orphans.
